# Palette: viridis for the primary scale, magma for the second one.
v_dark <- "#440154"; v_blue <- "#31688e"; v_teal <- "#21918c"; v_green <- "#5ec962"
m_pink <- "#b73779"; m_purple <- "#8c2981"; m_orange <- "#fc8961"
mse <- function(y, pred) mean((y - pred)^2)
pin <- function(u, tau) u * (tau - (u < 0))   # the pinball loss
# NHANES (data note: data/nhanes.md): adults with every column used here recorded, split at random
# 4,000 training, 3,000 tuning; the rest is the test set, not used.
nh <- NHANESraw |>

  select(Diabetes, Gender, Age, Race1, Poverty, Weight, Height, BMI, Pulse, BPSysAve, TotChol, DirectChol, PhysActive) |>

         active = as.numeric(PhysActive == "Yes"))
set.seed(310)   # the deck's one seed: the split, then every random step below, in order
nh_id <- sample(nrow(nh))
nh_train <- nh[nh_id[1:4000], ]
nh_tune  <- nh[nh_id[4001:7000], ]
nh_test  <- nh[nh_id[7001:nrow(nh)], ]
# Simulated data for parts 1 and 2, the same as the note's: noise that grows with x.
f_sim <- function(x) 3 + x + 2 * sin(x)
s_sim <- function(x) 0.5 + 0.35 * x
sim <- function(n) tibble(x = runif(n, 0, 10)) |> mutate(y = f_sim(x) + s_sim(x) * rnorm(n))
het_train <- sim(1000)
het_fresh <- sim(2000)
x_grid <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 201))
# The causality lecture's diagram of the adjustment theorem.
dag_adjust <- function(intervened = FALSE, title = NULL) {
  s <- if (intervened) '{ Z [pos="1,1"] T [pos="0,0"] Y [pos="2,0"] Z -> Y T -> Y }' else
                       '{ Z [pos="1,1"] T [pos="0,0"] Y [pos="2,0"] Z -> T Z -> Y T -> Y }'
  dag(s) %>% tidy_dagitty() %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
    geom_dag_point(size = 15, colour = "#e5ecf6") +
    geom_dag_text(size = 8, colour = v_dark) +
    geom_dag_edges(edge_width = 1.3) +
    expand_limits(x = c(-0.35, 2.35), y = c(-0.4, 1.45)) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_dag_blank() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, hjust = 0.5, colour = v_dark))
}
# A causal diagram with three nodes (plotmath labels), drawn by hand, in the convention of Loftus, Bynum and
# Hansen (2024): solid arrows for relations in the world, dashed arrows from the inputs to the prediction.
# Edges in order: left -> top, top -> right, left -> right.
dag3 <- function(labs3, ltys, title) {
  nodes <- tibble(x = c(0, 1.2, 2.4), y = c(0, 1, 0), lab = labs3)
  arw <- arrow(length = unit(0.12, "inches"), type = "closed")
  ggplot() +
    annotate("segment", x = 0.2, y = 0.18, xend = 0.95, yend = 0.8, linewidth = 1.1, colour = v_dark, arrow = arw, linetype = ltys[1]) +
    annotate("segment", x = 1.45, y = 0.8, xend = 2.2, yend = 0.18, linewidth = 1.1, colour = v_dark, arrow = arw, linetype = ltys[2]) +
    annotate("segment", x = 0.32, y = 0, xend = 2.08, yend = 0, linewidth = 1.1, colour = v_dark, arrow = arw, linetype = ltys[3]) +
    geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = lab), parse = TRUE, size = 7, label.size = 0.3,
               label.padding = unit(0.35, "lines")) +
    labs(title = title) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.4, 2.8), ylim = c(-0.3, 1.25), clip = "off") + theme_void() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 17, hjust = 0.5, colour = v_dark))
}

## Where we left off {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: which loss makes the best prediction the 90th percentile?

The title slide's question first: two minutes of answers, then this table. The title slide has no note, so its minutes are counted here. Then the question in the box; the answer is the next two slides.
:::

| Loss | Best prediction at $x$ | |
|---|---|---|
| Squared error, $(y - \hat y)^2$ | the conditional mean, $\mathbb E[Y \mid X = x]$ | optimal model theorem |
| Absolute error, $\lvert y - \hat y \rvert$ | the conditional median | stated |
| A miss costs $c_{FN}$, a false alarm $c_{FP}$ | predict $1$ when $p(x) > c^\star = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}$ | optimal threshold theorem |

**Decision principle**: choose the prediction $\hat y$ that minimizes the expected loss given the inputs, $\mathbb E[\ell(Y, \hat y) \mid X = x]$

::: {.ask}
Squared loss gives the mean, absolute loss the median. Which loss makes the best prediction the 90th percentile?
:::

### Part 1: decisions and quantiles

## Finding the quantile {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
The answer to the question, built up. Count who gains and who loses when the prediction moves up a little. The approximation: the outcomes between y-hat and y-hat + delta change sides, and with no probability at any single point their share vanishes as delta shrinks; that is where continuity enters.
:::

Charge $\tau$ for each unit of underprediction ($y > \hat y$) and $1 - \tau$ for each unit of overprediction ($y < \hat y$). Move the prediction up from $\hat y$ to $\hat y + \delta$:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- an outcome above $\hat y$: its loss falls by $\tau\delta$
- an outcome below $\hat y$: its loss rises by $(1 - \tau)\delta$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| label: heuristic-density
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 2.0
# A right-skewed density with a prediction y-hat marked: below it, the share F(y-hat); above it, 1 - F(y-hat).
a0 <- 4.2
dens <- tibble(y = seq(0, 14, length.out = 400)) |> mutate(d = dgamma(y, shape = 3, rate = 0.6))
ggplot(dens, aes(y, d)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(dens, y <= a0), fill = m_pink, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_area(data = filter(dens, y >= a0), fill = v_teal, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_vline(xintercept = a0, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = a0, y = 0.265, label = "hat(y)", parse = TRUE, size = 6, hjust = -0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 0.05, label = "F(hat(y))", parse = TRUE, colour = "black", size = 5.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 8.6, y = 0.10, label = "1 - F(hat(y))", parse = TRUE, colour = "black", size = 5.5) +
  labs(x = "y", y = NULL) + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```
:::
:::

With $F$ the distribution function of $Y$ given $X = x$, the expected change is about
$$
\delta\,\big[(1 - \tau)F(\hat y) - \tau\,(1 - F(\hat y))\big] = \delta\,\big[F(\hat y) - \tau\big]
$$

Keep moving up while $F(\hat y) < \tau$; stop where $F(\hat y) = \tau$: the **$\tau$-quantile**. For the 90th percentile, $\tau = 0.9$

## Quantile optimality

::: {.notes}
The loss of the last slide, as a function of the error y - y-hat. Stated here; the proof is a pre-seminar exercise (the heuristic, made exact: g(b) - g(a) is the integral of F - tau from a to b). Continuity gives a point where F = tau; if F is flat at tau, every point with F = tau minimizes; finiteness needs E|Y| finite.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
**Pinball loss**:
$$
\rho_\tau(y - \hat y) = (y - \hat y)\,\big(\tau - \mathbf 1\{y < \hat y\}\big)
$$
$\tau\,(y - \hat y)$ for an underprediction, $(1 - \tau)(\hat y - y)$ for an overprediction. With $\tau = \frac12$, half the absolute error
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
```{r}
#| label: pinball-plot
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 2.7
expand_grid(u = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 201), tau = c(0.5, 0.9)) |>
  mutate(loss = pin(u, tau)) |>
  ggplot(aes(u, loss, colour = factor(tau))) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`0.5` = v_dark, `0.9` = v_teal), name = expression(tau)) +
  labs(x = expression(y - hat(y)), y = "loss")
```
:::
:::

::: {.leave}
**Quantile optimality theorem.** If $Y \mid X = x$ has a continuous distribution and $0 < \tau < 1$, then $\arg\min_{\hat y} \mathbb E[\rho_\tau(Y - \hat y) \mid X = x]$ is the conditional $\tau$-quantile $q_\tau(x)$
:::

Squared loss gave the mean; half the absolute error, $\tau = \frac12$, gives the median

## Quantile regression

::: {.notes}
Empirical risk minimization with the pinball loss. rq() solves it as a linear program (quantreg, this deck only). Dashed: the true quantiles, known because we simulated. The lines fan out with the noise and miss the curvature.
:::

Minimize the average pinball loss over a class: $\hat q_\tau = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} \frac1n \sum_i \rho_\tau\big(y_i - f(x_i)\big)$. Here $\mathcal F$ is linear; 1,000 simulated points whose noise grows with $x$

```{r}
#| label: qr-linear-show
#| echo: true
fit_qr <- rq(y ~ x, tau = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), data = het_train)
```

```{r}
#| label: qr-linear-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-align: center
taus <- c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)
true_q <- map_dfr(taus, function(t) mutate(x_grid, tau = t, q = f_sim(x) + s_sim(x) * qnorm(t)))
lin_q <- map_dfr(seq_along(taus), function(k) mutate(x_grid, tau = taus[k], q = predict(fit_qr, x_grid)[, k]))
q_cols <- c(`0.05` = m_pink, `0.5` = v_dark, `0.95` = v_teal)
ggplot(het_train, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = true_q, aes(y = q, colour = factor(tau)), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = lin_q, aes(y = q, colour = factor(tau)), linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = q_cols, name = expression(tau)) + labs(x = "x", y = "y")
```

## The same loss, a flexible model

::: {.notes}
Any learner that takes a loss can fit a quantile. xgboost's objective reg:quantileerror is the pinball loss; depth 2, rate 0.05, 300 iterations, leaves of at least 30 points, one fit per tau, not tuned. The negative gradient of the pinball loss in the fitted value is tau minus the indicator: each tree fits signs, not residuals.
:::

Boosted trees with the pinball loss: each tree fits the negative gradient $\tau - \mathbf 1\{y_i < \hat f(x_i)\}$, which pushes the fit up where points lie above it

```{r}
#| label: qr-boost-show
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
xgboost(x, y, objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = 0.95, max_depth = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: qr-boost-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 2.75
#| fig-align: center
# The code shown above, for each tau, with the rest of the settings.
boost_q <- function(tau) xgboost(x = as.matrix(het_train["x"]), y = het_train$y,
  objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = tau,
  max_depth = 2, learning_rate = 0.05, nrounds = 300, min_child_weight = 30, nthread = 1)
fit_bq <- map(taus, boost_q)
boost_curve <- map_dfr(seq_along(taus), function(k) mutate(x_grid, tau = taus[k], q = predict(fit_bq[[k]], as.matrix(x_grid))))
ggplot(het_train, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = true_q, aes(y = q, colour = factor(tau)), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = boost_curve, aes(y = q, colour = factor(tau)), linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = q_cols, name = expression(tau)) + labs(x = "x", y = "y")
```

::: {.retrieval}
Boosting: each small tree approximates the negative gradient of the training loss
:::

### Part 2: regression uncertainty and intervals

## Two kinds of interval

::: {.notes}
lm()'s predict() with interval = "confidence" and "prediction", 90 percent, on a straight line with constant noise. The confidence band shrinks with n; the prediction band stays about as wide as the noise.
:::

At a new $x_0$, $Y_0 = f^\star(x_0) + \varepsilon_0$

- **Confidence interval** for $f^\star(x_0)$ (dark): uncertainty about the fit; it narrows as $n$ grows
- **Prediction interval** for $Y_0$ (light): must also cover $\varepsilon_0$; it does not narrow below the noise

```{r}
#| label: ci-pi
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| fig-align: center
# A straight line with constant noise; lm's 90% confidence and prediction intervals at two sample sizes.
ci_pi <- function(n) {
  d <- tibble(x = runif(n, 0, 10)) |> mutate(y = 1 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(n))
  fit <- lm(y ~ x, d)
  g <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 101))
  ci <- predict(fit, g, interval = "confidence", level = 0.9)
  pr <- predict(fit, g, interval = "prediction", level = 0.9)
  panel <- factor(paste0("n = ", format(n, big.mark = ",")), levels = c("n = 30", "n = 1,000"))
  list(d = mutate(d, panel = panel),
       g = mutate(g, fit = ci[, "fit"], cl = ci[, "lwr"], cu = ci[, "upr"], pl = pr[, "lwr"], pu = pr[, "upr"], panel = panel))
}
cp <- list(ci_pi(30), ci_pi(1000))
cp_g <- bind_rows(cp[[1]]$g, cp[[2]]$g); cp_d <- bind_rows(cp[[1]]$d, slice_sample(cp[[2]]$d, n = 300))
ggplot(cp_g, aes(x)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pl, ymax = pu), fill = v_teal, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = cl, ymax = cu), fill = v_dark, alpha = 0.55) + geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = v_dark) +
  geom_point(data = cp_d, aes(y = y), size = 0.8, alpha = 0.4) + facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "y") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

::: {.retrieval}
Bias--variance at $x_0$: $\sigma^2 + \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance}$; more data shrink only the variance
:::

## An interval from two quantiles

::: {.notes}
Three 90 percent intervals on the simulated data. Constant width: lm's prediction interval. Mean and variance: lm for the mean, then the absolute residuals regressed on x, scaled by sqrt(pi/2), times 1.645. Quantiles: the boosted fits. Dashed: the true 5 and 95 percent quantiles.
:::

A 90% interval from two quantile fits: $\hat C(x) = [\hat q_{0.05}(x), \hat q_{0.95}(x)]$. The true quantiles would cover $Y$ with probability $0.9$ at every $x$; estimated ones aim at that

```{r}
#| label: three-intervals
#| include: false
z90 <- qnorm(0.95)
fit_lm <- lm(y ~ x, het_train)
fit_abs <- lm(abs(resid(fit_lm)) ~ x, het_train)
interval_fns <- list(
  `constant width` = function(d) { p <- predict(fit_lm, d, interval = "prediction", level = 0.9); cbind(p[, "lwr"], p[, "upr"]) },
  `mean and variance` = function(d) { m <- predict(fit_lm, d); s <- predict(fit_abs, d) * sqrt(pi / 2); cbind(m - z90 * s, m + z90 * s) },
  `linear quantiles` = function(d) predict(fit_qr, d)[, c(1, 3)],
  `boosted quantiles` = function(d) cbind(predict(fit_bq[[1]], as.matrix(d["x"])), predict(fit_bq[[3]], as.matrix(d["x"])))
)
bands <- imap_dfr(interval_fns, function(fn, nm) { b <- fn(x_grid); tibble(x = x_grid$x, lo = b[, 1], hi = b[, 2], method = nm) }) |>
  mutate(method = fct_inorder(method))
true_band <- x_grid |> mutate(lo = f_sim(x) - z90 * s_sim(x), hi = f_sim(x) + z90 * s_sim(x))
```

```{r}
#| label: three-intervals-plot
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(filter(bands, method != "linear quantiles"), aes(x)) +
  geom_point(data = het_train, aes(y = y), alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = v_teal, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = true_band, aes(y = lo), linetype = "dashed") + geom_line(data = true_band, aes(y = hi), linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ method) + labs(x = "x", y = "y") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

## Checking an interval on fresh data {minutes="3"}

```{r}
#| label: coverage
#| include: false
cov_methods <- c("constant width", "mean and variance", "boosted quantiles")
cov_pts <- imap_dfr(interval_fns[cov_methods], function(fn, nm) {
  b <- fn(het_fresh)
  tibble(method = nm, x = het_fresh$x, y = het_fresh$y, lo = b[, 1], hi = b[, 2],
         inside = het_fresh$y >= b[, 1] & het_fresh$y <= b[, 2], width = b[, 2] - b[, 1])
}) |> mutate(method = factor(method, levels = cov_methods))
cov_all <- cov_pts |> group_by(method) |> summarise(all = mean(inside), width = mean(width))
# Five ranges of x, about 400 fresh points each; a range's coverage is outside the band if it is more than
# two binomial standard errors from 90%.
cov_rng <- cov_pts |> mutate(mid = 2 * floor(pmin(x, 9.999) / 2) + 1) |>
  group_by(method, mid) |> summarise(cov = mean(inside), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
se2 <- 2 * sqrt(0.9 * 0.1 / mean(cov_rng$n))
cov_rng <- cov_rng |> mutate(off = abs(cov - 0.9) > se2)
pct <- function(v) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * v)
```

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: we claim 90 percent intervals; how do you check, and what could the check miss?

Two minutes, then the plot. Fresh data: 2,000 new points from the same simulation, used for nothing else. Grey: the interval; pink points fall outside it. Above each panel, the coverage in each range of width 2, about 400 points each; pink when more than two binomial standard errors (3 points) from 90 percent. Mean widths `r sprintf("%.1f", cov_all$width[1])`, `r sprintf("%.1f", cov_all$width[2])`, `r sprintf("%.1f", cov_all$width[3])`; the true quantiles' `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(2 * z90 * s_sim(het_fresh$x)))`. Coverage by range is a diagnostic, not a certificate: a range can still hide a subgroup.
:::

::: {.ask}
We claim 90 percent intervals. With fresh data in hand, how do you check the claim, and what could the check miss?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: coverage-plot
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-align: center
y_lab <- max(cov_pts$y) + 2
ggplot(cov_pts, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = arrange(cov_pts, method, x), aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = inside), size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(2, 4, 6, 8), colour = "grey70", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_text(data = cov_rng, aes(x = mid, y = y_lab, label = pct(cov), fontface = if_else(off, "bold", "plain")),
            colour = if_else(cov_rng$off, m_pink, "grey30"), size = 4.6, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey45", `FALSE` = m_pink), labels = c(`TRUE` = "inside", `FALSE` = "outside"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, 2)) + coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "fresh y") +
  theme(legend.position = "right", strip.text = element_text(size = 16), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Overall: `r pct(cov_all$all[1])`, `r pct(cov_all$all[2])` and `r pct(cov_all$all[3])`; a wider interval always covers more
:::

## Coverage at every $x$

::: {.notes}
Stated, not proved. Nontrivial: in the paper (Proposition 2.2) a procedure with that guarantee has infinite expected length at almost every x that is not an atom. Wording rule: finite samples, conditional on X = x, every distribution with nonatomic inputs; group-conditional and assumption-based results remain possible.
:::

- **Marginal coverage**: $P\big(Y \in \hat C(X)\big) \ge 1 - \alpha$, averaged over $X$
- **Conditional coverage**: $P\big(Y \in \hat C(X) \mid X = x\big) \ge 1 - \alpha$ for every $x$

::: {.leave}
**Impossibility of distribution-free conditional coverage.** No procedure has a nontrivial finite-sample guarantee of coverage conditional on $X = x$ that holds for every distribution with nonatomic inputs (Barber et al. 2021). Guarantees for groups (each range of $x$, say), and results under assumptions or as $n$ grows, remain possible
:::

::: {.retrieval}
No free lunch theorem: no method does best on every distribution; a guarantee at every $x$ needs an assumption about the distribution
:::

## Conformalized quantile regression {minutes="3"}

```{r}
#| label: cqr
#| include: false
# Boosted 5% and 95% fits on the first 500 training points; scores on the other 500 (m = 500).
fit_part <- 1:500; cal_part <- 501:1000
m_cal <- length(cal_part); k90 <- ceiling(0.9 * (m_cal + 1))
boost_half <- function(tau) xgboost(x = as.matrix(het_train[fit_part, "x"]), y = het_train$y[fit_part],
  objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = tau,
  max_depth = 2, learning_rate = 0.05, nrounds = 300, min_child_weight = 30, nthread = 1)
b05_half <- boost_half(0.05); b95_half <- boost_half(0.95)
plug_in <- function(d) cbind(predict(b05_half, as.matrix(d["x"])), predict(b95_half, as.matrix(d["x"])))
cal <- het_train[cal_part, ]
b_cal <- plug_in(cal)
cal$score <- pmax(b_cal[, 1] - cal$y, cal$y - b_cal[, 2])
Q_cqr <- sort(cal$score)[k90]
b_fresh <- plug_in(het_fresh)
in_plug <- het_fresh$y >= b_fresh[, 1] & het_fresh$y <= b_fresh[, 2]
in_cqr <- het_fresh$y >= b_fresh[, 1] - Q_cqr & het_fresh$y <= b_fresh[, 2] + Q_cqr
in_68 <- het_fresh$x > 6 & het_fresh$x <= 8
b_own <- plug_in(het_train[fit_part, ])
cover_own <- mean(het_train$y[fit_part] >= b_own[, 1] & het_train$y[fit_part] <= b_own[, 2])
```

::: {.notes}
Romano, Patterson and Candès (2019), section 4: the score is their equation 6, Q their equation 8, the interval their equation 7. The fits cover `r pct(cover_own)` of their own training points and `r pct(mean(cal$score <= 0))` of the calibration rows, so Q is positive. Why, if asked: a new row is inside exactly when its score is at most Q; the fits saw neither the calibration rows nor the new row, so the m + 1 scores are exchangeable, the new one's rank is uniform on 1 to m + 1 (no ties), and P(rank at most k) = k/(m + 1). One mean fit for both ends makes the score |y − f-hat(x)|: split conformal prediction.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="64%"}
1. Fit $\hat q_{0.05}$, $\hat q_{0.95}$ on some training rows; keep $m$ others, the **calibration set**
2. Score how far each $y_i$ is outside (negative inside): $E_i = \max\{\hat q_{0.05}(x_i) - y_i,\ y_i - \hat q_{0.95}(x_i)\}$
3. $Q$: the $\lceil 0.9\,(m + 1) \rceil$-th smallest score
4. $\hat C(x) = \big[\hat q_{0.05}(x) - Q,\ \hat q_{0.95}(x) + Q\big]$
:::
::: {.column width="36%"}
```{r}
#| label: cqr-plot
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(cal, aes(x, score)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = score > Q_cqr), size = 1.3, alpha = 0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = Q_cqr, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("label", x = 0, y = Q_cqr, label = "Q", size = 5.5, hjust = 1.4, label.size = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey50", `TRUE` = m_pink)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "score")
```
:::
:::

::: {.leave}
**Conformal coverage theorem** (Romano et al. 2019). If the calibration rows and a new row are exchangeable, $P(Y \in \hat C(X)) \ge 0.9$ for any quantile fits, and $\le 0.9 + 1/(m + 1)$ if the scores have no ties
:::

$m = `r m_cal`$, $Q = `r sprintf("%.2f", Q_cqr)`$: coverage `r pct(mean(in_plug))` to `r pct(mean(in_cqr))`; for $x$ in 6–8, `r pct(mean(in_plug[in_68]))` to `r pct(mean(in_cqr[in_68]))`. One $Q$ for all $x$

## Ways to make an interval {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: each method assumes something and claims a kind of coverage; the note on the course page has this table and how each works.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.72em"}
| Method | Assumes | Can claim |
|---|---|---|
| Linear model, normal noise (`predict(lm, interval = "prediction")`) | linear mean, constant variance, normal noise | 90% at every $x$, if the model is right |
| A model for the mean and one for the variance | both models right, normal noise | about 90% at every $x$, if right |
| Quantile regression, linear or flexible | the quantile model right | 90% at every $x$ as $n$ grows, if right |
| Split conformal prediction (Lei et al. 2018) | rows exchangeable, e.g. independent and from one distribution | at least 90% marginally, in finite samples; the same width at every $x$ |
| Conformalized quantile regression (Romano et al. 2019) | rows exchangeable | at least 90% marginally, in finite samples; widths from the quantile fits |
:::

More in the note on the course page, "Prediction intervals and calibration"

## {.inverse .center}

::: {.notes}
Compress: a probability is calibrated when it matches a frequency; check it on fresh data; recalibrate on rows not used to fit.
:::

### Part 3: classification uncertainty and calibration

## A probability should match a frequency {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: a model gives p-hat = 0.2 to 500 adults; what should be true of them?

About 100 should have diabetes. Coverage and calibration are the same idea: a stated probability is a frequency. Calibration conditions on the score's value, not on x.
:::

::: {.ask}
A model gives $\hat p = 0.2$ to 500 adults: their probability of having diabetes. What should be true of them?
:::

. . .

About 100 of them should have diabetes. A score $\hat p$ is **calibrated** if
$$
P\big(Y = 1 \mid \hat p(X)\big) = \hat p(X)
$$

The same idea as coverage: a stated probability should match a frequency. It conditions on the score, not on $x$

## Reliability diagram

::: {.notes}
Diabetes as reported in the survey. Nine inputs: age, sex, BMI, pulse, systolic blood pressure, total and HDL cholesterol, the income-to-poverty ratio, physical activity; race and ethnicity left out (they return on "Calibrated within groups"). xgboost with its defaults (depth 6, rate 0.3, 100 iterations). Ten bins of equal size by p-hat: 300 tuning adults or 400 training adults each. On the adults who fitted it, the boosted score looks too cautious at the top; on fresh adults it is too confident.
:::

```{r}
#| label: calibration-fits
#| include: false
cal_inputs <- c("Age", "male", "BMI", "Pulse", "BPSysAve", "TotChol", "DirectChol", "Poverty", "active")
fit_lr <- glm(diabetes ~ Age + male + BMI + Pulse + BPSysAve + TotChol + DirectChol + Poverty + active,
              family = binomial, data = nh_train)
fit_xg <- xgboost(x = as.matrix(nh_train[cal_inputs]), y = factor(nh_train$diabetes), nthread = 1)   # defaults: depth 6, rate 0.3, 100 iterations
p_lr <- predict(fit_lr, nh_tune, type = "response")
p_xg <- predict(fit_xg, as.matrix(nh_tune[cal_inputs]))
p_xg_train <- predict(fit_xg, as.matrix(nh_train[cal_inputs]))
y_tune <- nh_tune$diabetes
# Bins with equal numbers of adults, by the score's value.
reliability <- function(p, y, bins = 10) tibble(p, y) |>
  mutate(bin = ntile(p, bins)) |>
  group_by(bin) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_p = mean(p), freq = mean(y), .groups = "drop")
base_rate <- mean(nh_train$diabetes)
```

Diabetes (`r round(100 * base_rate)`% of the training adults). Two scores from nine measurements, fitted on 4,000 adults, checked on 3,000 others

```{r}
#| label: reliability-plot
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center
rel <- bind_rows(
  reliability(p_lr, y_tune) |> mutate(score = "logistic regression", rows = "tuning adults"),
  reliability(p_xg, y_tune) |> mutate(score = "boosted trees", rows = "tuning adults"),
  reliability(p_xg_train, nh_train$diabetes) |> mutate(score = "boosted trees", rows = "training adults")) |>
  mutate(score = fct_inorder(score))
ggplot(rel, aes(mean_p, freq, colour = rows)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.6) + facet_wrap(~ score) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`tuning adults` = v_dark, `training adults` = "grey60"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = c("0", "0.5", "1")) + coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "predicted probability (bin average)", y = "share with diabetes") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16), legend.position = "right")
```

## Calibration and the threshold

::: {.notes}
The base rate is calibrated: given the score (always the same), the frequency is the base rate. With a calibrated score, the optimal threshold theorem applies with the score as the only input. A miscalibrated score needs its own cut, which is what recalibration finds.
:::

- The base rate, $\hat p(x) = `r sprintf("%.2f", base_rate)`$ for every adult, is calibrated, and useless: calibration says nothing about how well a score separates those with diabetes from the rest
- If $\hat p$ is calibrated, predicting $1$ when $\hat p(x) > c^\star$ is the best rule **based on that score**: the optimal threshold theorem, with $\hat p(X)$ as the input. It is the Bayes rule only if $\hat p = p$
- If $\hat p$ is not calibrated, $c^\star$ is the wrong cut on it

::: {.retrieval}
Optimal threshold theorem: with costs $c_{FP}$ and $c_{FN}$, the rule that minimizes expected cost at $x$ predicts $1$ exactly when $p(x) > c^\star = c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})$
:::

## Recalibration

::: {.notes}
A logistic regression of the label on the logit of the boosted score, fitted on the first 1,500 tuning adults, checked on the other 1,500. Increasing in p-hat when b is positive, so the ranking is unchanged. Five bins of 300 adults here.
:::

```{r}
#| label: recalibration
#| include: false
half_a <- 1:1500; half_b <- 1501:3000
logit_p <- function(p) qlogis(pmin(pmax(p, 1e-4), 1 - 1e-4))
recal <- glm(y ~ s, family = binomial, data = tibble(y = y_tune[half_a], s = logit_p(p_xg[half_a])))
p_recal <- predict(recal, tibble(s = logit_p(p_xg[half_b])), type = "response")
b_recal <- coef(recal)[["s"]]
logloss <- function(p, y) -mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
```

Fit $\tilde p = 1/\big(1 + e^{-(a + b\,\mathrm{logit}\,\hat p)}\big)$ by a logistic regression of the label on $\mathrm{logit}\,\hat p = \log\frac{\hat p}{1 - \hat p}$, on adults not used to fit $\hat p$ (half the tuning adults); check on others (the other half)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: recalibration-plot
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.8
bind_rows(reliability(p_xg[half_b], y_tune[half_b], 5) |> mutate(score = "boosted"),
          reliability(p_recal, y_tune[half_b], 5) |> mutate(score = "recalibrated")) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_p, freq, colour = score)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(boosted = "grey55", recalibrated = v_dark), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "predicted probability", y = "share with diabetes") + theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Fitted $b = `r sprintf("%.2f", b_recal)`$: the boosted logits shrunk by about half

$\tilde p$ is increasing in $\hat p$ (for $b > 0$): the same ranking, new probabilities

Log loss on the checking adults: `r sprintf("%.3f", logloss(p_xg[half_b], y_tune[half_b]))` before, `r sprintf("%.3f", logloss(p_recal, y_tune[half_b]))` after
:::
:::

## Calibrated within groups

```{r}
#| label: multicalibration
#| include: false
# The logistic score of the reliability diagram (race and ethnicity left out), by the survey's five groups.
groups_of <- function(d) c(list(everyone = rep(TRUE, nrow(d))),
                           setNames(lapply(levels(d$Race1), function(l) d$Race1 == l), levels(d$Race1)))
by_group <- function(d, p) imap_dfr(groups_of(d), function(g, nm) tibble(
  group = nm, n = sum(g), observed = mean(d$diabetes[g]), predicted = mean(p[g]))) |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(observed * (1 - observed) / n))
grp <- by_group(nh_tune, p_lr) |> mutate(group = fct_inorder(group))
# Multicalibration, in the spirit of Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018), section 3.2: for each group and each tenth of
# the score's range with at least 100 adults, if the share with diabetes and the average score differ by more
# than the tolerance, shift the scores there by the difference; repeat until none does.
multicalibrate <- function(p, y, groups, tol = 0.02, min_n = 100, max_rounds = 200) {
  shifts <- list()
  for (r in seq_len(max_rounds)) {
    moved <- FALSE
    for (g in names(groups)) for (v in 0:9) {
      cell <- groups[[g]] & pmin(floor(10 * p), 9) == v
      if (sum(cell) < min_n) next
      gap <- mean(y[cell]) - mean(p[cell])
      if (abs(gap) > tol) { p[cell] <- pmin(pmax(p[cell] + gap, 0.001), 0.999); moved <- TRUE
        shifts[[length(shifts) + 1]] <- list(g = g, v = v, gap = gap) }
    }
    if (!moved) break
  }
  list(p = p, shifts = shifts)
}
# The shifts found on one half, applied in the same order to the other half.
apply_shifts <- function(p, groups, shifts) {
  for (s in shifts) { cell <- groups[[s$g]] & pmin(floor(10 * p), 9) == s$v; p[cell] <- pmin(pmax(p[cell] + s$gap, 0.001), 0.999) }
  p
}
tune_a <- nh_tune[half_a, ]; tune_b <- nh_tune[half_b, ]
mcal <- multicalibrate(p_lr[half_a], tune_a$diabetes, groups_of(tune_a))
p_mc_b <- apply_shifts(p_lr[half_b], groups_of(tune_b), mcal$shifts)
mc_b <- by_group(tune_b, p_lr[half_b]) |> mutate(after = by_group(tune_b, p_mc_b)$predicted)
```

::: {.notes}
Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold and Rothblum (2018), definition 2.6 and section 3.2. Bars: plus or minus two binomial standard errors. Tried here on half the tuning adults (tolerance 0.02, tenths of the score, cells of at least 100), checked on the other half: `r length(mcal$shifts)` shifts; White `r sprintf("%.3f", mc_b$predicted[mc_b$group == "White"])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", mc_b$after[mc_b$group == "White"])` (observed `r sprintf("%.3f", mc_b$observed[mc_b$group == "White"])`), Black `r sprintf("%.3f", mc_b$predicted[mc_b$group == "Black"])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", mc_b$after[mc_b$group == "Black"])` (observed `r sprintf("%.3f", mc_b$observed[mc_b$group == "Black"])`); log loss `r sprintf("%.3f", logloss(p_lr[half_b], tune_b$diabetes))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", logloss(p_mc_b, tune_b$diabetes))`. Small cells: the shifts fit noise too.
:::

Calibrated overall, wrong within groups. **Multicalibration** (Hébert-Johnson et al. 2018): calibrated within every group of a collection named in advance

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| label: multicalibration-plot
#| fig-width: 6.8
#| fig-height: 3.7
ggplot(grp, aes(y = fct_rev(group))) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = observed - 2 * se, xmax = observed + 2 * se), height = 0.25, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(x = observed, colour = "share with diabetes"), size = 3.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = predicted, colour = "average score"), shape = 17, size = 3.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`share with diabetes` = "black", `average score` = m_pink), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "tuning adults", y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
The logistic score above (race and ethnicity left out), 3,000 tuning adults, the survey's groups

The fix: where a group's share of 1s in a range of scores is off by more than a tolerance, shift those scores; repeat. Small cells fit noise; a group not named gets no guarantee
:::
:::

## {.inverse .center}

::: {.notes}
Compress: plots of a fitted model describe the model; partial dependence, ICE and Shapley values for any model; importance by permuting or leaving out.
:::

### Part 4: interpreting the model

## Partial dependence for any model

```{r}
#| label: pd-helpers
#| include: false
pd_curve <- function(fit, d, v, grid) map_dbl(grid, function(t) { nd <- d; nd[[v]] <- t; mean(predict(fit, nd)) })
# The simulated interaction of the ensembles lecture: x1 enters only through its product with a function of x2.
f1 <- function(x) x^2
f2 <- function(x) cos(pi * x / 2)
df_int <- tibble(x1 = runif(2000, -1, 1), x2 = runif(2000, -4, 4)) |>
  mutate(y = f1(x1) * f2(x2) + rnorm(2000))
```

::: {.notes}
Notation from Loftus, Bynum and Hansen (2024), without their prime. The PDP is a computation on f-hat: set, leave, predict, average. For an additive f-hat it is the component plus a constant. Wording rule: ICE evaluates f-hat at a modified input that may correspond to no plausible unit. The last line closes the causality seminar's note on recomputing each unit with its own noise.
:::

Options for the other inputs: hold them fixed (at medians, say: `plotmo`'s default); average over them (partial dependence, `pdp`); one curve for each unit (individual conditional expectation, ICE)

Unit $i$'s inputs with input $j$ set to a value $\tilde x_j$: $\;\tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij} = (x_{i1}, \ldots, \tilde x_j, \ldots, x_{ip})$
$$
\mathrm{ICE}_i:\ \tilde x_j \mapsto \hat f(\tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij}), \qquad
\mathrm{PDP}_j:\ \tilde x_j \mapsto \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \hat f(\tilde{\mathbf x}_{ij})
$$

Compute on a grid of $\tilde x_j$ values and plot the curve(s). Any model that predicts will do

ICE evaluates $\hat f$ at a modified input, which may correspond to no plausible unit. It is the model's prediction there, not what would have happened to unit $i$: recomputing a unit with its own noise, as in the causality seminar, asks a different kind of question, which this course does not develop

## A forest fits interactions; its partial dependence plot {minutes="1"}

::: {.notes}
A forest on the simulated interaction, every input offered at every split (bagging); nodes under 50 units not split. Flat, like the GAM's curve for x_1 last time. Does the forest ignore x_1? Next slide.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rf-ice
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_int, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 50)
ice_x1 <- partial(fit_rf, pred.var = "x1", ice = TRUE, train = df_sub)
```

```{r}
#| label: rf-pdp-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: 56%
#| fig-align: center
# The code shown above, on 100 of the 2,000 units, and the plot.
fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_int, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 50)
df_sub <- df_int |> slice_sample(n = 100) |> mutate(yhat.id = row_number(), sign = if_else(f2(x2) > 0, "positive", "negative"), strength = f2(x2)^4)
ice_x1 <- partial(fit_rf, pred.var = "x1", ice = TRUE, train = as.data.frame(df_sub[, c("x1", "x2")]), grid.resolution = 30) |>
  as_tibble() |> left_join(df_sub |> select(yhat.id, sign, strength), by = "yhat.id")
pdp_x1 <- ice_x1 |> group_by(x1) |> summarise(yhat = mean(yhat), .groups = "drop")
ice_ylim <- range(ice_x1$yhat)
ggplot(pdp_x1, aes(x1, yhat)) +
  geom_line(colour = "black", linewidth = 1.8) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = ice_ylim) + labs(x = "x1", y = "prediction")
```

Black: the PDP, the forest's prediction averaged over 100 units with $x_1$ set and $x_2$ left at each unit's value. Nearly flat

## A forest fits interactions; its ICE curves

::: {.notes}
The same slide with the ICE curves. Solid teal: units with cos(pi x_2 / 2) > 0; dashed orange: < 0. The GAM's x_1 curve was flat too, but the GAM has no interaction to hide; only the ICE curves tell the two apart.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rf-ice-shown-again
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_int, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 50)
ice_x1 <- partial(fit_rf, pred.var = "x1", ice = TRUE, train = df_sub)
```

```{r}
#| label: rf-ice-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: 56%
#| fig-align: center
# The same forest, curves and axes as on the last slide, with the ICE curves added.
ggplot(ice_x1, aes(x1, yhat)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = yhat.id, colour = sign, linetype = sign, alpha = strength), linewidth = 0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = pdp_x1, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(positive = v_teal, negative = m_orange)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(positive = "solid", negative = "dashed")) +
  scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.03, 0.75), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = ice_ylim) + labs(x = "x1", y = "prediction")
```

Thin: one curve per unit (ICE), solid where $\cos(\pi x_2/2) > 0$, dashed where it is negative, more opaque the larger $|\cos(\pi x_2/2)|$. The forest fitted the interaction, PDP hides it, and ICE might show it

## Shapley values

```{r}
#| label: shapley-forest
#| include: false
# Exact Shapley values for two inputs, on 300 units that are also the background data. v(S): the inputs in S at
# the unit's values, the other input at every background unit's value, the forest's predictions averaged.
sh_units <- df_int |> slice_sample(n = 300)
cross <- expand_grid(i = 1:300, j = 1:300) |>
  mutate(x1 = sh_units$x1[i], x2 = sh_units$x2[j]) |>
  mutate(pred = predict(fit_rf, pick(x1, x2)))
v1 <- cross |> group_by(i) |> summarise(v = mean(pred)) |> pull(v)          # x1 known: average over x2
v2 <- cross |> group_by(j) |> summarise(v = mean(pred)) |> pull(v)          # x2 known: average over x1
v0 <- mean(cross$pred); v12 <- predict(fit_rf, sh_units)
sh_units <- sh_units |> mutate(phi1 = 0.5 * ((v1 - v0) + (v12 - v2)),
                               sign = if_else(f2(x2) > 0, "positive", "negative"), strength = f2(x2)^4)
# The forest's PDP for x1 on the same 300 units, minus the average prediction.
pd_grid <- tibble(x1 = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 30)) |>
  mutate(pd1 = pd_curve(fit_rf, as.data.frame(sh_units[c("x1", "x2")]), "x1", x1) - v0)
```

::: {.notes}
Shapley's value from cooperative game theory, used to split a prediction; IML's chapter on SHAP if anyone asks. Computed exactly here for two inputs, 300 units of the simulated interaction, the same forest. With independent inputs the average Shapley value at x_1 is the PDP minus the average prediction; the spread is the interaction. Efficiency: the shares add up to the prediction minus the average prediction.
:::

Split a prediction among the inputs, $\hat f(\mathbf x_i) - v_i(\varnothing) = \phi_{i1} + \dots + \phi_{ip}$; $v_i(S)$ predicts from the inputs in $S$ only (usually: the others averaged over the data, as in partial dependence). For two inputs, adding $x_1$ in either order (for $p$, all $p!$ orders):
$$
\phi_{i1} = \tfrac12\Big[\big(v_i(\{1\}) - v_i(\varnothing)\big) + \big(v_i(\{1, 2\}) - v_i(\{2\})\big)\Big]
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: shapley-forest-plot
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 2.6
ggplot(sh_units, aes(x1, phi1)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = sign, shape = sign, alpha = strength), size = 1.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = sign), method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = pd_grid, aes(y = pd1), linewidth = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(positive = v_teal, negative = m_orange)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(positive = 16, negative = 1)) +
  scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.15, 0.9), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.6, 0.6)) +
  labs(x = "x1", y = expression(phi[1]))
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
The forest; 300 units shaded as the ICE curves, a smooth for each sign: the spread shows the interaction. Black: the PDP minus the average prediction, the Shapley values' average when inputs are independent
:::
:::

## Feature/variable "importance"

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, with a forest for systolic blood pressure on NHANES adults (nine inputs, 300 trees, mtry = 3 fixed for the refits two slides on). Split improvement is randomForest's IncNodePurity; permutation is on the tuning adults, the forest unchanged, ten shuffles each. Each measure as a share of its total over the nine inputs, so the two share an axis. Weight, height and BMI: BMI is weight over height squared.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rf-bp
#| include: false
# A forest for systolic blood pressure from nine inputs; BMI is weight / height^2, so three inputs are tied.
imp_inputs <- c("Age", "Gender", "Race1", "Weight", "Height", "BMI", "Pulse", "TotChol", "Poverty")
rf_bp <- randomForest(BPSysAve ~ Age + Gender + Race1 + Weight + Height + BMI + Pulse + TotChol + Poverty,
                      data = nh_train, ntree = 300, mtry = 3)
```

- Which predictors are *used most* by the model?
- Does not necessarily tell us about **causation** (none of these methods do)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
#### Tree-specific importance

Sum the RSS decrease of every split on $x_j$ within a tree, then average over trees

#### Permutation importance

Permute values of predictor $x_j$. How much does the accuracy of the model decrease?
$$\mathrm{PI}_j = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f, x_j \text{ permuted}) - \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f)$$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| label: importance
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-height: 3.15
base_tune <- mse(nh_tune$BPSysAve, predict(rf_bp, nh_tune))
pi_j <- sapply(imp_inputs, function(v) mean(replicate(10, {
  d <- nh_tune; d[[v]] <- sample(d[[v]]); mse(nh_tune$BPSysAve, predict(rf_bp, d)) })) - base_tune)
split_j <- importance(rf_bp)[imp_inputs, "IncNodePurity"]
tibble(input = factor(imp_inputs, levels = imp_inputs[order(split_j)]),
       `split improvement` = split_j / sum(split_j), permutation = pi_j / sum(pi_j)) |>
  pivot_longer(-input, names_to = "measure") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, input, colour = measure, shape = measure)) + geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`split improvement` = v_dark, permutation = m_pink), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`split improvement` = 15, permutation = 17), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "share of the measure's total", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.margin = ggplot2::margin(0, 0, -8, 0), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 13))
```

Each has pros/cons, no satisfactory answer for dependence
:::
:::

## Permutation and extrapolation

```{r}
#| label: permute-counts
#| include: false
# Height shuffled once among the tuning adults; weight and BMI stay. BMI from weight (kg) and height (cm).
perm <- nh_tune |> mutate(Height = sample(Height))
bmi_from <- function(d) d$Weight / (d$Height / 100)^2
off <- function(d) mean(abs(d$BMI - bmi_from(d)) > 2)
short_heavy <- function(d) sum(d$Height < 155 & d$Weight > 110)
```

::: {.notes}
The tuning adults, height shuffled once. Hooker, Mentch and Zhou (2021): with dependent inputs, shuffling puts weight where there are few data, in importance and in partial dependence alike; a PDP for height sets it on every adult, whatever their weight and BMI.
:::

```{r}
#| label: permute-height
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-align: center
bind_rows(nh_tune |> mutate(data = "tuning adults"),
          perm |> mutate(data = "height permuted")) |>
  mutate(data = fct_inorder(data), from = bmi_from(pick(everything()))) |>
  ggplot(aes(from, BMI)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1, colour = v_blue) +
  facet_wrap(~ data) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 80), ylim = c(15, 70)) +
  labs(x = "weight / height squared", y = "recorded BMI") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

Shuffling height keeps each adult's weight and BMI: BMI no longer matches weight and height for `r round(100 * off(perm))`% of them (`r round(100 * off(nh_tune))`% before); `r short_heavy(perm)` are under 155 cm and over 110 kg (`r short_heavy(nh_tune)` before)

The forest's predictions there rest on almost no data, and permutation importance averages over them (Hooker, Mentch and Zhou 2021)

## Permutation with correlated inputs {.inverse}

```{r}
#| label: biv-perm
#| include: false
n_biv <- 400; rho_biv <- -0.8
b1 <- rnorm(n_biv); b2 <- rho_biv * b1 + sqrt(1 - rho_biv^2) * rnorm(n_biv)
biv <- tibble(x1 = b1, x2 = b2); biv_perm <- tibble(x1 = b1, x2 = sample(b2))
biv_lims <- c(-3.6, 3.6)
biv_kde <- MASS::kde2d(biv$x1, biv$x2, n = 120, lims = c(biv_lims, biv_lims))
biv_grid <- expand_grid(x2 = biv_kde$y, x1 = biv_kde$x) |> mutate(z = as.vector(t(biv_kde$z)))
biv_breaks <- c(0.002, 0.01, 0.03, 0.06, 0.1, 0.15, 0.3)
dens_at <- function(x, y) biv_kde$z[cbind(pmax(findInterval(x, biv_kde$x), 1), pmax(findInterval(y, biv_kde$y), 1))]
low_perm <- mean(dens_at(biv_perm$x1, biv_perm$x2) < 0.01); low_data <- mean(dens_at(biv$x1, biv$x2) < 0.01)
```

::: {.notes}
Compress: permuting one of two correlated inputs puts many points where the model has seen almost no data. x_1, x_2 standard normal with correlation -0.8; both panels shade the density estimated from the data on the left.
:::

```{r}
#| label: biv-perm-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
#| dark: true
biv_panel <- function(d, title) ggplot() +
  geom_contour_filled(data = biv_grid, aes(x1, x2, z = z), breaks = biv_breaks, alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = d, aes(x1, x2), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "mako", direction = -1, begin = 0.15) +
  coord_equal(xlim = biv_lims, ylim = biv_lims, expand = FALSE) + labs(title = title, x = "x1", y = "x2") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 17))
biv_panel(biv, "the data, and their density") + biv_panel(biv_perm, "x2 permuted, the same density")
```

Where the data's density is below 0.01: `r round(100 * low_perm)`% of the permuted points, `r round(100 * low_data)`% of the data

## Leave one covariate out

::: {.notes}
Ten more forests, mtry = 3 as in the full one: one per input left out, one without weight, height and BMI; all scored on the tuning adults. For an additive f with independent inputs, permuting x_j adds 2 Var f_j(X_j) to the error, refitting without it Var f_j(X_j). Two questions: how much the fitted model relies on x_j; what the method loses without it. IML calls it LOFO.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: loco
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
refit_without <- function(drop) {
  fit <- randomForest(reformulate(setdiff(imp_inputs, drop), "BPSysAve"), data = nh_train, ntree = 300, mtry = 3)
  mse(nh_tune$BPSysAve, predict(fit, nh_tune)) - base_tune
}
loco_j <- sapply(imp_inputs, refit_without)
loco_body <- refit_without(c("Weight", "Height", "BMI"))
tibble(input = imp_inputs, permutation = pi_j, LOCO = loco_j) |>
  pivot_longer(-input, names_to = "importance") |>
  mutate(input = fct_reorder(input, value, .fun = max)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, input, colour = importance, shape = importance)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(LOCO = v_blue, permutation = m_pink), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(LOCO = 16, permutation = 17), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "increase in tuning MSE", y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
Refit without input $j$, with the same settings; score on the same held-out adults (Lei et al. 2018):
$$\mathrm{LOCO}_j = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}\big(\hat f^{(-j)}\big) - \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f)$$

No extrapolation from permuting; any method, at the cost of $p$ refits

Weight, height and BMI together: `r sprintf("%.1f", loco_body)`, more than the three alone added up (`r sprintf("%.1f", loco_j[["Weight"]])`, `r sprintf("%.1f", loco_j[["Height"]])`, `r sprintf("%.1f", loco_j[["BMI"]])`). Any two give the third
:::
:::

## Marginal or conditional Shapley values

::: {.notes}
Chen, Janizek, Lundberg and Lee (2020), "True to the model or true to the data?": marginal is their interventional, conditional their observational. The example, if asked: v(empty) = 0, v({1}) = v({1, 2}) = beta_1 x_1, and v({2}) = beta_1 E[X_1 | x_2] = beta_1 rho x_2; the formula on the last slide gives the rest. Which to use depends on the question; neither is a causal effect: that is part 5.
:::

$v_i(S)$ must fill in the inputs not in $S$ (Chen et al. 2020):

- **Marginal**: from the data, ignoring $\mathbf x_{iS}$, as in partial dependence. True to the model: an input $\hat f$ ignores gets $0$; but $\hat f$ is evaluated where there may be no data, as in permutation
- **Conditional**: $v_i(S) = \mathbb E\big[\hat f(X) \mid X_S = \mathbf x_{iS}\big]$. True to the data; but an input $\hat f$ ignores gets a share through the inputs correlated with it, and the conditional distribution must be estimated

::: {.fragment}
Example: $\hat f(\mathbf x) = \beta_1 x_1$; inputs with mean $0$, variance $1$, correlation $\rho$, and $\mathbb E[X_1 \mid x_2] = \rho x_2$. Marginal: $\phi_{i2} = 0$. Conditional: $\phi_{i2} = \frac12 \rho \beta_1 x_{i2}$, and $\phi_{i1} = \beta_1 x_{i1} - \phi_{i2}$
:::

## {.inverse .center}

::: {.notes}
Compress: a plot of the model answers a question about the model; a question about the world needs a causal model and a model that is right about the world.
:::

### Part 5: the model and the world

## Predictions and outcomes {minutes="3"}

```{r}
#| label: world
#| include: false
# The world of this part (simulated): x1 causes x2, and both cause y. The fitted model: least squares on x1 and x2.
n_w <- 2000
x2_eq <- function(x1) x1 + rnorm(length(x1), 0, 0.5)
world <- tibble(x1 = rnorm(n_w)) |> mutate(x2 = x2_eq(x1), y = x1 + 2 * x2 + rnorm(n_w))
fit_w <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = world)
b_w <- coef(fit_w)
```

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: to let x_2 respond when we change x_1, what do we need besides the fitted model?

A causal model for the inputs: how x_2 depends on x_1. The ECM is Loftus, Bynum and Hansen (2024), Definition 2.5, drawn as in their figures: solid arrows in the world, dashed arrows into the prediction; the real outcome is not in it (their Remark 2.12). Simulated: x_1 standard normal, x_2 = x_1 plus normal noise with sd 0.5, y = x_1 + 2 x_2 plus standard normal noise; 2,000 units. Fitted coefficients `r sprintf("%.2f", b_w[["x1"]])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", b_w[["x2"]])`.
:::

::: {.ask}
A partial dependence plot for $x_1$ leaves $x_2$ at each unit's value. In the world, $x_2$ responds to $x_1$. To let it respond, what do we need besides the fitted model?
:::

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
A causal model for the inputs. An **explanatory causal model** (ECM; Loftus, Bynum and Hansen 2024) adds the prediction $\hat Y = \hat f(X)$, with the fitted model as its equation

The outcome $Y$ is not in it: questions about $Y$ also need $\hat f$ to be right about the world

Here $x_2 = x_1 + \varepsilon_2$ and $y = x_1 + 2x_2 + \varepsilon$; $\hat f$ is least squares on $x_1$ and $x_2$
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
```{r}
#| label: ecm-dags
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 3.4
dag3(c("x[1]", "x[2]", "y"), c("solid", "solid", "solid"), "The world (simulated)") /
  dag3(c("x[1]", "x[2]", "hat(y)"), c("solid", "dashed", "dashed"), "The ECM")
```
:::
:::

## Natural direct and total dependence {minutes="3"}

```{r}
#| label: tdp
#| include: false
t_grid <- seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = 51)
avg_pred <- mean(predict(fit_w))
nddp <- pd_curve(fit_w, world, "x1", t_grid)
# Total dependence: set x1 to t for every unit, draw x2 again from its equation in the ECM, predict, average.
tdp <- map_dbl(t_grid, function(t) mean(predict(fit_w, mutate(world, x1 = t, x2 = x2_eq(rep(t, n_w))))))
# Shapley values for x1 on 300 units. The fit is linear, so v(S) is the fit at the expected inputs. Marginal: the
# others at their averages in the data. Conditional: the world is known, so E[X2 | x1] = x1 and E[X1 | x2] = 0.8 x2.
fw <- function(x1, x2) b_w[["(Intercept)"]] + b_w[["x1"]] * x1 + b_w[["x2"]] * x2
sh_w <- world |> slice_sample(n = 300) |> mutate(
  marginal = 0.5 * ((fw(x1, mean(world$x2)) - fw(mean(world$x1), mean(world$x2))) + (fw(x1, x2) - fw(mean(world$x1), x2))),
  conditional = 0.5 * ((fw(x1, x1) - fw(0, 0)) + (fw(x1, x2) - fw(0.8 * x2, x2))))
slope_cond <- coef(lm(conditional ~ x1, sh_w))[["x1"]]
```

::: {.notes}
NDDP and TDP: their Definitions 2.9 and 2.7; PDP with ICE = NDDP is their Theorem 2.10, on the model's output, not the outcome. We draw the averages only; the paper also draws a curve for each unit. Shapley values are centered, so the curves are drawn minus the average prediction. Conditional, if asked: phi_1 = 2 x_1 − 0.4 x_2 with coefficients 1 and 2, about 1.6 x_1 on the data. Causal Shapley values here give 2 x_1: the direct part, x_1, and half of the indirect part through x_2.
:::

In the ECM, set $x_1 = t$ for every unit, predict, average, with $x_2$

- left at each unit's value: the **natural direct dependence plot** (NDDP), which is the PDP
- recomputed from its equation: the **total dependence plot** (TDP), $\mathbb E[\hat f(X) \mid do(x_1 = t)]$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| label: tdp-plot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.9
dep <- tibble(t = t_grid, NDDP = nddp - avg_pred, TDP = tdp - avg_pred) |> pivot_longer(-t, names_to = "plot")
sh_long <- sh_w |> pivot_longer(c(marginal, conditional), names_to = "Shapley") |>
  mutate(Shapley = factor(Shapley, levels = c("marginal", "conditional")))
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = sh_long, aes(x1, value, shape = Shapley), colour = "grey35", size = 1.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = dep, aes(t, value, colour = plot), linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(NDDP = m_pink, TDP = v_blue), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(marginal = 16, conditional = 2), name = "Shapley") +
  labs(x = "x1", y = "centered")
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
Slopes: NDDP `r sprintf("%.1f", b_w[["x1"]])`, TDP `r sprintf("%.1f", b_w[["x1"]] + b_w[["x2"]])`. Marginal Shapley values for $x_1$ lie on the NDDP; conditional ones, slope `r sprintf("%.1f", slope_cond)`, on neither

**Causal Shapley values** (Heskes et al. 2020) put $do(\cdot)$ in place of conditioning
:::
:::

## Model-intervention corollary {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Stated; the notebook derives it from the adjustment theorem with the two errors. Wording rule: a population identity, which the PDP estimates; an estimate even when f-hat = f-star. Model error: the average of f-hat minus f-star at (t, z_i); sampling error: the average of f-star(t, z_i) minus its expectation over Z. Say: with no consequence of T among the inputs, the NDDP and the TDP are the same plot. Zhao and Hastie (2021) made this link between partial dependence and adjustment.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
::: {.leave}
**Model-intervention corollary.** Let $f^\star(t, z) = \mathbb E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]$. If $Z$ holds every common cause of $T$ and $Y$ and no consequence of $T$, and $P(T = t \mid Z) > 0$, then $\mathbb E_Z\big[f^\star(t, Z)\big] = \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)]$
:::
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
```{r}
#| label: corollary-dag
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-height: 3.3
dag_adjust(FALSE, "as observed") / dag_adjust(TRUE, "under do(T = t)")
```
:::
:::

A population identity: the adjustment theorem, written with $f^\star$. The PDP $\frac1n\sum_i \hat f(t, z_i)$ estimates it, an estimate even when $\hat f = f^\star$:
$$
\mathrm{PDP}_T(t) = \mathbb E[Y \mid do(T = t)] + \text{model error} + \text{sampling error}
$$

## Where the condition fails {minutes="3"}

```{r}
#| label: fails
#| include: false
fit_w2 <- lm(y ~ x2, data = world)
# The effects, from the simulation's equations: do(x1 = t) lets x2 respond, so E[Y] = t + 2t;
# do(x2 = t) leaves x1 alone, so E[Y] = E[X1] + 2t = 2t.
fails <- bind_rows(
  tibble(x = t_grid, PDP = pd_curve(fit_w, world, "x2", t_grid), effect = 2 * t_grid,
         case = "x2; x1 in the model:\nthe condition holds"),
  tibble(x = t_grid, PDP = nddp, effect = 3 * t_grid,
         case = "x1; x2 in the model:\na consequence of x1 held fixed"),
  tibble(x = t_grid, PDP = pd_curve(fit_w2, world, "x2", t_grid), effect = 2 * t_grid,
         case = "x2; x1 left out:\na common cause missing")) |>
  mutate(case = fct_inorder(case))
slope_w2 <- coef(fit_w2)[["x2"]]
```

::: {.notes}
The effects come from the simulation's equations, which we know. Left: the corollary's condition holds, and the PDP tracks the effect. Middle: the direct path only, slope `r sprintf("%.1f", b_w[["x1"]])` against 3. Right: x_1 causes both x_2 and y; leave it out and the slope for x_2 is `r sprintf("%.1f", slope_w2)` against 2 (in the population, Cov(Y, X_2)/Var(X_2) = 3.5/1.25 = 2.8). Every curve is still a correct statement about its f-hat.
:::

Partial dependence (pink) against the effect of setting the plotted input (dashed), in the simulated world

```{r}
#| label: fails-plot
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(fails, aes(x)) + geom_line(aes(y = PDP), colour = m_pink, linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = effect), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ case) +
  labs(x = "value set for the plotted input", y = "y") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 14))
```

::: {.retrieval}
Adjustment theorem: every common cause of $T$ and $Y$, and **no consequence** of $T$
:::

## History: asthma and pneumonia {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Skip if behind. Caruana et al. (2015), section 1, pp. 1721 to 1722, read through a summary of the PDF; the study it recounts is from the mid 1990s.
:::

- In the 1990s, models predicted the risk of death from pneumonia, to decide who should be admitted to hospital
- A rule learned from the data: patients with asthma had a **lower** risk
- The reason: asthmatic patients with pneumonia were usually admitted straight to intensive care, and the care worked
- The rule was a correct description of the data. Acting on it would have sent patients with asthma home
- The most accurate model, a neural network, was not used: nobody could check what else it had learned (Caruana et al. 2015)

## Conclusion {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: the loss decides the target; check intervals and probabilities on fresh data and across the range; a plot of the model describes the model, and an effect needs a causal model and a model that is right.
:::

#### Uncertainty

The loss decides which number is the best prediction; two quantiles make an interval, and conformalizing them guarantees marginal coverage. Check coverage and calibration on data not used to fit, across the range of the inputs and within groups: no method guarantees coverage at every $x$ without assumptions

#### Interpretation

Partial dependence, ICE, Shapley values and importance describe $\hat f$. A curve is an effect only when no input is a consequence of the plotted one and every common cause is in the model; with a causal model for the inputs, the total dependence plot answers a different question
